newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico corp Q2 results show light at end of tunnel.
newsitem.headline: Mexico corp Q2 results show light at end of tunnel.

text.p: Mexican companies have turned in their best quarterly results since the 1994 peso crisis, heralding for most firms the long-awaited light at the end of the recessionary tunnel.
Second quarter results released over the past few days showed sales finally picking up at home after a two-year slump and export volumes continuing to boom despite a strong peso.
"The numbers were a marked improvement over the past quarters," said Damian Fraser, director at Caspian Research in Mexico City.
The results were good enough to endorse the Mexican stock market's recent rally during May and June, but were not good enough to justify big new gains, analysts said.

"The market has priced in quite a lot of the potential upside. Certaintly the pace of gains will have to slow down," said Lars Schonander, head of equity research at Santander Investment in Mexico City.
But results marked a clear turnaround from the first quarter, when domestic sales remained sluggish and exports were slowing in the face of peso strength.
"What is clear from these results is the recovery of the domestic market," said Ricardo Peon, director of analysis at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Mexico City.
Sales rose on average more than five percent compared with the year-ago quarter, while operating profits rose nearly eight percent, according to analysts.
Net profits were on average lower, but that was due to a non-cash accounting item that revalues a company's debt according to inflation.
Because inflation was much lower during the past quarter than during the same time last year, companies notched up less of the invisible gain.
Media companies, retailers and beverage firms were the clearest winners. Media giant Grupo Televisa saw its television advertising sales jump 26 percent compared with the year-ago quarter.

Beverage companies also did well. Pepsi Co's anchor bottler in Mexico, Pepsi-Gemex, turned in its best quarter since the devaluation, with sales up 15.5 percent in real terms compared with the first quarter.

In the retail sector, the news was more mixed. Mexico's biggest retailer Cifra posted a disappointing one percent growth in same-store sales, while Soriana continued to rack up an impressive performance.

"The retailers may have to wait until the third or fourth quarter to start to show that the consumer is really back," said James Barrineau, head of Latin American equity strategy at Smith Barney in New York.
Construction and cement firms were less impressive.
Nearly all posted weak sales growth, except for cement giant Cemex SA, which was helped by its foreign operations.
Export companies did well despite a peso that has gained in real terms against the dollar and made Mexican goods sold abroad more expensive.
Conglomerate Desc's second quarter revenues grew 16.5 percent, while industrial giant Alfa used export volume growth to offset a strong peso and price weakness for some of its commodities.

"Export growth appears less dependent on the exchange rate than imports," said Schonander, who said companies nonetheless are switching some of their sales to the domestic market because of higher margins.
